entry.content:
1 minute read
ASUS XG Core RX 9060 XT LP: specs and price
2:36

ASUS's XG Core is a USB4 graphics box with a Radeon RX 9060 XT LP and 16 GB of GDDR6. A UK listing shows £2,999.

We’re a bit late on this one, but it’s interesting enough for a more detailed look all the same. ASUS has announced the XG Core Radeon RX 9060 XT LP 16GB GDDR6, an external graphs card enclosure that adds graphics power to compatible laptops, gaming handhelds, and mini PCs. Connecting via USB4, with up to 40 Gbps bandwidth, it’s driven by a Radeon RX 9060 XT LP GPU graphics card based on AMD RDNA 4 architecture, with 16 GB of GDDR6 memory.

Effectively, that gives you an impressive amount of fast graphics grunt without the need for any internal modifications to your setup. That matters on a thin laptop or a compact PC, where internal upgrades are often not even physically possible.

The unit measures a compact 144 x 117 x 39 mm (5.7 x 4.6 x 1.5 in) and has built-in HDMI and DisplayPort outputs for working on larger screens. Named supported hosts unsurprisingly include the ROG Ally X and ROG Xbox Ally X, and it also supports compatible Thunderbolt 3 systems. Power is via USB-C.

It enables GPU acceleration in video editing, 3D rendering, and design applications that can use the Radeon GPU. Given the usefulness of GPUs when it comes to processing AI instructions, it also lets you run local AI image generation and LLM inference in compatible software such as ComfyUI, LM Studio, and Ollama.

Clock speeds and AI performance

Performance and software compatibility depend on the workload, model, and system configuration, and though you won’t get the same performance as with a standalone desktop Radeon RX 9060 XT, it is still impressive. ASUS quotes 406.3 AI TOPS (INT4 matrix sparsity) and a default mode boost clock up to 1600 MHz (and game clock up to 1010 MHz).

ASUS GPU Tweak III provides controls for GPU core clocks, memory frequency, voltage, and fan control, plus real-time monitoring and a customizable on-screen display.

Pricing and availability

The XG Core Radeon RX 9060 XT LP 16GB GDDR6 is still rolling out, but we found a UK pricing of £2999. That typically translates into $2999, though tariffs can complicate matters further. We’ll update when we know more.

entry.title: Beeble SwitchX 3.0: new features and availability
entry.summary: 1 minute read Beeble SwitchX 3.0: new features and availability 2:41 Beeble's SwitchX 3.0 video-to-video model now takes up to four reference images, with improved camera tracking and prompt control. Beeble has launched SwitchX 3.0, billed as a major update to its AI-powered vide
entry.content:
1 minute read
Beeble SwitchX 3.0: new features and availability
2:41

Beeble's SwitchX 3.0 video-to-video model now takes up to four reference images, with improved camera tracking and prompt control.

Beeble has launched SwitchX 3.0, billed as a major update to its AI-powered video-to-video model that allows users to alter filmed environments in post.

SwitchX 3.0 adds four updates that cover support for up to four visual references, dynamic backgrounds, improved camera tracking, and more precise prompt control.

Dynamic backgrounds, multiple references

With dynamic backgrounds, the generated environment now reacts to the shot, allowing users to add explosions, moving fire, and falling snow as the video above shows. The addition of multiple references adds what the company says is the most requested feature since launch. For example, artists can now use a wide shot of the whole set, a close-up of a prop, and a storyboard, and combine them together to create the final video.

As ever, Beeble's proprietary Source-Locked Rendering technology preserves the original performance within an actor's alpha matte, frame by frame, while changing the surrounding environment and lighting.

Beeble says camera tracking was good in version 2.0 and is improved again in 3.0, handling handheld and orbiting moves. The company says the generated background stays locked to the world as if it had been there during the shoot, with no tracking markers or matchmove pass required.

Beeble says better prompt control lets users describe what happens in the scene, how it moves, and when. This theoretically is going to make using it feel more like directing a scene rather than just generating backgrounds.

Specs and availability

SwitchX 3.0 is built on MiniMax H3.0 and has been re-engineered using Beeble's own dataset and architecture. It supports up to 4K output with 10-bit color, retaining frame count and aspect ratio from the source footage. It is, however, capped at 360 frames per video, down from 480 frames in SwitchX 2.0, which is 15 seconds against 20 seconds at 24 fps.

It is available globally through the Beeble web app and Canvas, with no change to existing credit pricing. It is included in all paid plans, with 4K and 10-bit MOV downloads available to Professional and Team subscribers. Creator costs $19 a month ($16 billed annually) and Professional $75 a month ($60 billed annually). As ever, AI costs are a fairly complex moving picture of different credits and capabilities so check https://beeble.ai/pricing-cloud for more info.

entry.summary: 2 minute read Nikon Z70: rumored specs, price and release date 3:07 Nikon's Z70 looks set for announcement within weeks. Leaks point to a 41 MP APS-C body with 8K60 video, IBIS, and a price around $2000. There is nothing official about the Nikon Z70, not even a teaser video as ye
entry.content:
2 minute read
Nikon Z70: rumored specs, price and release date
3:07

Nikon's Z70 looks set for announcement within weeks. Leaks point to a 41 MP APS-C body with 8K60 video, IBIS, and a price around $2000.

There is nothing official about the Nikon Z70, not even a teaser video as yet, but there is plenty of anticipation that something is coming imminently. Over the past three months, a fairly consistent picture of a fast, video-capable APS-C body has been built up by a succession of leaked materials from a range of sources, most of it documented by the industrious Nikon Rumors. Here is the story so far.

How the Z70 first leaked

The name first surfaced on August 8, when a "Nikon Z70" appeared on Apple's list of authorized ProRes and ProRes RAW cameras, just below the Z6 III. It was gone within hours, leaving only the Z6 III, Z8, Z9, and ZR.

On October 29, Nikon Rumors posted a screenshot said to come from Nikon Singapore, promoting the new NIKKOR Z 120-300mm f/2.8 TC VR S lens. The caption reads: "Pair with the Z70's Digital Teleconverter and reach stretches to an equivalent of 1,260mm at f/4."

Then, on November 4, Nikon registered a new wireless remote, the N2416, with the FCC. Drawings in its manual show a camera that matches no current Nikon mirrorless body, with an extra button beside the top LCD. The next day, Nikon Rumors said it could confirm that the camera was the Z70 and that the new button is for recording.

Nikon Z70 rumored specs

All unconfirmed so far
  • Sensor: 41 MP, not stacked. Earlier reports had suggested 45 MP and stacked.
  • Processor: Expeed 7.
  • Video: 8K60, ProRes RAW support, and "RED tech inside."
  • Stabilization: IBIS.
  • Viewfinder: the Z6 III's 5.76 million-dot EVF.
  • Digital teleconverter: a new mode, which fits the Nikon Singapore caption.
  • Controls: a dedicated REC button on the top plate.
  • Price: in the $2000 ballpark.

What it means for video shooters

Last year's ZR was the first RED co-branded Nikon camera, and is even commonly referred to as the RED ZR nowadays. But by the looks of the rumored spec sheet, the Z70 would take the video capabilities even further. ProRes RAW, a REC button, and 8K video signal some serious intent, and would make it a competitive choice for video work, especially at that $2000 price point. It could conceivably even be branded the RED Z70, at least in some markets.

When will the Nikon Z70 be announced?

That is less clear. It seems to have originally been expected in August or September, but has slipped. It is, of course, not the only camera to do so. Fujifilm's X-T6 went so far as to have a launch event penciled in before disappearing from the schedules, and it is still AWOL.

The new NIKKOR Z 120-300mm f/2.8 TC VR S was announced October 29, though, and is due to hit the market in mid-November, i.e., now. We know of at least one major camera that is being announced next week too, so we could be in for a busy end of the year.

entry.title: Insta360 X5 in How to Rob a Bank: 360 camera use
entry.summary: 2 minute read Insta360 X5 in How to Rob a Bank: 360 camera use 3:30 Up to 20 Insta360 X5 cameras ran at once on 'How to Rob a Bank' heist footage, with the production able to reframe 360-degree action shots in post to change perspectives. The Insta360 X5 makes its Hollywood film
entry.content:
2 minute read
Insta360 X5 in How to Rob a Bank: 360 camera use
3:30

Up to 20 Insta360 X5 cameras ran at once on 'How to Rob a Bank' heist footage, with the production able to reframe 360-degree action shots in post to change perspectives.

The Insta360 X5 makes its Hollywood film debut today with the release of How to Rob a Bank, an action film directed by David Leitch (Bullet Train, The Fall Guy). The film stars Nicholas Hoult, Zoë Kravitz, Anna Sawai, Rhenzy Feliz, Christian Slater, Pete Davidson, and John C. Reilly, and follows a crew of social media-savvy bank robbers who broadcast their heists on socials. Think Robin Hood retooled for Gen Z.

How the heist crew's footage was shot

The X5 is the camera the crew uses in the story to document their exploits, and while normal 35mm cinematography captures much of the movie, the heist videos within the film use the X5 footage itself.

Reframing 360 footage

Jimmy Johenning, producer of digital sequences, demonstrated reframing to director Leitch and Jonathan Sela, director of photography for the main unit, on an iPad in pre-production. And for Leitch, the ability to create new shots from existing 360 footage proved particularly valuable during the heist sequences. Essentially it gave the team more flexibility to connect the action and keep the story moving. As he explains, “When we needed a shot and we had a 360 running, we could literally create a shot.”

Post production supervisor Jacob Donohue gives an example: a shot that looks down the barrel of a gun could be reframed later to show the person holding it. The team typically ran seven or eight X5 cameras per shooting day, with 12 to 20 during individual heist sequences. On motorcycles and moving vehicles, filmmakers shaped camera movements in post that would have been difficult or effectively impossible to execute physically at those speeds.

FlowState Stabilization and 360° Horizon Lock were used on moving vehicles and actors for car scenes, motorcycles, and fight sequences.

New camera placements

The team also explored camera placements that would have been challenging to achieve with conventional setups. For Jonathan Sela, placing an X5 inside a money bag offered a particularly compelling perspective: the camera captured the robbers throwing cash into the bag, turning it around, and tossing it, bringing the audience directly into the action.

Another shot looks through a stack of banknotes as the robbers flip through the money, and is a favorite of Donohue. David Myrick, director of photography, of the film’s YouTube unit (yes, it has one of those), says that the cameras opened up possibilities beyond the familiar tools of dollies, Steadicams and cranes. “This was just kind of like there were no rules,” he says.

Lens losses and post

Film sets are not the safest places on earth, and the production went through approximately 20 to 30 lenses but only around two camera bodies, which is a decent casualty rate considering their use in action sequences.

As for post, the team first processed and reframed footage in Insta360 Studio, then transcoded to ProRes for DaVinci Resolve and Avid before cutting it in with the 35mm footage.

How to Rob a Bank is now playing in theaters and, while the reviews are lukewarm, the way that it uses 360 video seems fairly hot.

entry.title: Yamaha to acquire Disguise: what we know so far
entry.summary: 1 minute read Yamaha to acquire Disguise: what we know so far 1:27 Yamaha Corporation has decided to acquire virtual production specialist Disguise. Terms are undisclosed, and Disguise keeps its brand intact. Yamaha Corporation has decided to acquire Disguise, which has been busy
entry.content:
1 minute read
Yamaha to acquire Disguise: what we know so far
1:27

Yamaha Corporation has decided to acquire virtual production specialist Disguise. Terms are undisclosed, and Disguise keeps its brand intact.

Yamaha Corporation has decided to acquire Disguise, which has been busy over the past few years establishing an excellent reputation in virtual production and live events, touching everything from tours by Taylor Swift and Bad Bunny to films such as Project Hail Mary.

The company has won two Emmy Awards and has been owned by Carlyle for more than five years. Over the past decade, under CEO Fernando Küfer, it has grown from a media server specialist for concert touring into a platform spanning software, hardware, and creative and technical services.

Everything we know is fairly corporate at this point. A statement says that the acquisition is part of Yamaha’s strategy to grow beyond musical instruments and audio equipment. The combined company will expand into software and services for live entertainment, sports, and venues, cross-sell both portfolios, and develop more integrated solutions.

The Disguise brand and its customer and partner relationships will be preserved, and Disguise will become a new pillar alongside Yamaha’s existing business. Customers and partners will continue to work with the same Disguise teams.

More news on the combined roadmap will follow in 2027. No terms have been disclosed.

entry.title: Adobe MAX 2026 on demand: 13 video sessions
entry.summary: 5 minute read Adobe MAX 2026 on demand: 13 video sessions 9:14 Adobe MAX 2026 is now on demand. Here are 13 sessions worth your time if you work in video, from the Opening Keynote to the latest Adobe Labs sneaks. So, that is Adobe MAX over for another year. MAX 2026 in Miami feat
entry.content:
5 minute read
Adobe MAX 2026 on demand: 13 video sessions
9:14

Adobe MAX 2026 is now on demand. Here are 13 sessions worth your time if you work in video, from the Opening Keynote to the latest Adobe Labs sneaks.

So, that is Adobe MAX over for another year. MAX 2026 in Miami featured the usual huge number of sessions and panels, many of which are available on demand via Adobe's sessions page. We have picked 13, a baker's dozen that matter to video professionals. Of course, given the sheer volume of content available, the list is not comprehensive. It leans toward editing, color, and the experimental projects from Adobe Labs, with a couple of broader craft and creator rights sessions added.

Nine of the 13 are available to watch now and run for just under six hours combined, though much of that is taken up by the Opening Keynote and MAX Sneaks. Three of the shorter sessions below (the Premiere and After Effects demo, Project Deep Brush, and Project Rinse Repeat) are also cut from the Keynote and Sneaks, so you can jump straight to them if you're running short on time. Sessions that list their runtime as TBA are coming soon.

1. Opening Keynote

Speakers: Shantanu Narayen, Chair and CEO, Adobe; Anil Chakravarthy, President and incoming CEO, Adobe; and 10 more

Adobe's typically bravura main-stage opener brings together creative professionals and creators, who share workflow demos and videos, with Adobe executives discussing how to advance creativity and craft. Anna McNaught, Elise Swopes, and Paul Trani are among the Adobe evangelists on the speaker list. The Premiere and After Effects demo from this keynote is also available as its own session (number 4 below).

Key themes: Creative Cloud · Workflow demos · Executive vision · Creator tools

Runtime: 153 minutes

2. MAX Sneaks

Speakers: Terry Crews, award-winning actor and co-host; Kelsey Slay, Design Evangelist, Adobe; and 10 more

Sneaks is always box office at MAX and offers a first look at what Adobe's Labs teams are working on. The speaker list includes researchers such as Alberto Tono, Hyeonho Jeong, and Yiwei Hu. The individual projects are also published as shorter clips, and two of them, Project Deep Brush and Project Rinse Repeat, are covered at numbers 12 and 13 below. We've got the full Sneaks write-up on what was shown.

Key themes: Adobe Labs · Experimental tools · Future features

Runtime: 90 minutes

3. Beyond the Cut: How Great Editors Think

Speaker: Vinnie Hobbs, Film Editor, VH Post

Vinnie Hobbs's credits include award-nominated projects for Kendrick Lamar, Beyoncé, and Nicki Minaj. Here he looks at how design inside the timeline gives an edit its impact. Drawing on high-pressure music video and commercial workflows, he covers rhythm, composition, contrast, and visual hierarchy, including when to strip an edit back and when to push density. It is pitched at beginner and intermediate editors.

Key themes: Pacing and rhythm · Composition · Visual hierarchy · Music video workflows

Runtime: TBA

4. Premiere & After Effects: AI, Color & Audio

Speaker: Dacia Sáenz, Strategic Development Manager, Adobe

Sáenz is always good value at MAX, and here she tours new Premiere and After Effects features while making a film about life on the ocean. She removes a stray crew member from a shot, uses the AI assistant to mark interview questions, cleans up boat audio with stem separation, generates B-roll in the timeline, grades footage in the new Color mode, and animates text in After Effects.

Key themes: AI assistant · Stem separation · Generative B-roll · Color mode

Runtime: 11 minutes

5. Top 5 Things Creators Need to Know about Color Mode

Speaker: Karina Anglada, Strategic Development Manager, Adobe Pro Video

Anglada shares her tips for quick color correction in Premiere's Color mode: moving through clips efficiently, applying adjustments with precision, building looks you can reuse, and setting up color management so you start from the right place each time. It is a beginner-level session that uses traditional techniques rather than AI features.

Key themes: Color mode · Color correction · Reusable looks · Color management

Runtime: 18 minutes

6. 5 Premiere Tricks That Feel Like Magic

Speaker: Chris Hansen, Sr. Solutions Consultant, Adobe

Hansen takes a raw clip from rough cut to share-ready video in real time using Premiere's AI-assisted tools. The session covers text-based editing, automatic reframing for social, generative fixes for tricky shots, and one-click audio cleanup. Adobe pitches it at beginner and intermediate users.

Key themes: Text-based editing · Auto reframing · Generative fixes · Audio cleanup

Runtime: 21 minutes

7. Adobe Photoshop & After Effects for Premiere Editors

Speaker: John Knowles, Director, Editor, Designer, Trainer, Weirdsmobile Productions

Aimed at editors who have hit the limits of what they can do in Premiere, Knowles covers round-trip workflows between Premiere, Photoshop, and After Effects. Topics include designing Photoshop assets for motion, moving between apps with Dynamic Link, using motion tracking, parenting, and advanced keyframing in After Effects, and building revision-ready workflows with Render and Replace.

Key themes: Round-trip workflows · Dynamic Link · Motion tracking · Render and Replace

Runtime: TBA

8. Craft Cinematic Looks with Film Simulations for Photo & Video

Speaker: Rich Harrington, Omnichannel Strategy and Workflow Solutions, Fujifilm North America Corporation

Harrington follows a look from capture to output across stills and video. It starts with Fujifilm Film Simulations in camera, continues into Lightroom Classic and Adobe Camera Raw with Camera Matching Profiles for RAW photos, and ends in Premiere with LOG footage graded using Film Simulation LUTs. The aim is to create a matching look across photo and video from the same shoot.

Key themes: Film Simulations · Camera Matching Profiles · LOG and LUT workflow · Stills and motion

Runtime: TBA

9. Craft in the Age of AI: Preserving Your Creative Voice

Speaker: Martina Flor, Lettering Designer, Author and Educator, Studio Martina Flor

Flor uses her Futuremaker artwork, created for Adobe's Creative Collective, as a case study in combining analog craft, digital design, and AI-powered tools in a single process. She looks at where AI can accelerate the work and where human judgment, taste, and craft still make the difference. It is a general-audience session.

Key themes: Creative voice · Analog and digital craft · AI workflows · Authorship

Runtime: 16 minutes

10. High-Velocity Filmmaking: From Concept to Edit in Real Time by Drex Lee

Speakers: Drex Lee, Creative Pioneer & Viral Filmmaker; Devang Aggarwal, Staff Product Manager, Consumer Apps & AI Ecosystem - Compute, Qualcomm

A live stage demo of shooting, transferring, editing, and delivering short-form content in real time. It covers one-shot camera moves on mobile, wireless ingest of high-bitrate footage, agentic AI for finding the clips worth keeping, and Snapdragon-accelerated AI features in Premiere, which Adobe claims can cut editing time in half.

Key themes: Mobile capture · Wireless ingest · Agentic clip curation · On-device AI

Runtime: 35 minutes

11. Empowering Creators: Defining the Future of Creative Rights

Speakers: Karen Robinson, SVP, Deputy General Counsel, Adobe; Kent Keirsey, Director, Product - Firefly & Agentic, Adobe; Fabiola Lara, Illustrator + Content Creator, @FabiolitaDraws

A timely conversation on copyright, attribution, and creator rights in the age of AI, with Adobe's legal and product leads and a working illustrator. Topics include public policy efforts to protect creators, how creators, platforms, and policymakers can collaborate on regulation, and how Content Credentials, which Adobe describes as tamper-resistant, can attach attribution and show a creative process.

Key themes: Copyright · Attribution · Content Credentials · Policy

Runtime: TBA

12. Project Deep Brush

Speaker: Iliyan Georgiev, Senior Research Scientist, Adobe

This sneak centers on a model trained to separate images into physically decomposed layers, which then drive new painting tools. Generative AI works underneath, but Adobe says it is transparent to the artist. The applications shown include controlling paint placement, lighting-aware retouching, and lighting design.

Key themes: Adobe Labs · Layer decomposition · Lighting-aware control · Retouching

Runtime: 9 minutes

13. Project Rinse Repeat

Speaker: Ridam Batra, Senior Computer Scientist, Adobe

Strictly a stills tool, at least for now, but a very cool one. Project Rinse Repeat brings copy and paste to edits themselves. You capture the work done in one region of an image and paste it onto others, where it adapts to each target. Every edit is recreated with real Photoshop tools, so the results are non-destructive and can be refined.

Key themes: Adobe Labs · Repeatable edits · Non-destructive editing · Photoshop

Runtime: 6 minutes

entry.title: Adobe MAX 2026 Sneaks: all 10 projects
entry.summary: 3 minute read Adobe MAX 2026 Sneaks: all 10 projects 4:51 Adobe showed 10 experiments at MAX 2026 Sneaks. Project Deep Brush and Project Hands On are already open to try in the new Adobe Labs Playground. Always one of the most popular sessions at Adobe MAX , and one closely watch
entry.content:
3 minute read
Adobe MAX 2026 Sneaks: all 10 projects
4:51

Adobe showed 10 experiments at MAX 2026 Sneaks. Project Deep Brush and Project Hands On are already open to try in the new Adobe Labs Playground.

Always one of the most popular sessions at Adobe MAX, and one closely watched by the rest of the industry as well, the MAX Sneaks sessions showcase new tools that are just inching off Adobe’s R&D drawing board. Some tend to come to market in the following year, some disappear without a trace, and some go on to change Adobe’s product lineup and everyone else’s too.

You get the picture: Sneaks is impactful. You can watch a replay of the live stream here, and below we have a quick run through of the 10 research projects on display.

We also covered the 2025 Sneaks and the 2024 rundown.

 Adobe Labs Playground

Terry Crews hosted this year’s session, and for the first time some of the projects can be tried hands-on in the new Adobe Labs Playground. Two of the below projects are already on there, suggesting that they might be further on the road to full deployment than others: Project Deep Brush and Project Hands On. Also in the Playground is Project Custom Filters, a new capability for Photoshop that Adobe is exploring. Adobe is inviting the creative community to explore these and share feedback, with new projects billed as coming soon. Judging by the descriptions below, these will be Project Screen Test and Project Sound Bender.

To absolutely no one’s great surprise, most of these seem to involve AI tools in at least some if not all of the process.

Video

Project Scene Sweep

Editing video across multiple shots can mean repeating the same change again and again. Project Scene Sweep understands characters, locations, and scenes across a sequence, helping creators apply an edit consistently across cuts and camera angles. A creative decision is made once, then carried across a whole scene.

Project Screen Test

Project Screen Test lets creators develop a fictional character’s look, voice, and personality, then have a natural language dialogue with that character to explore who they are and how they might respond in different scenes.

Project Live Set

Project Live Set lets creators change a subject, transform an environment, or redirect the camera as a scene continues.

Project On Cue

A video prompt can describe what happens, but what about when? Project On Cue lets creators direct the timing of an action, like a flash of light or another event, in generated video. An editable timing signal can be drawn by hand or extracted from a video or piece of music, making it possible to bring motion and sound together on cue.

Audio

Project Sound Bender

Project Sound Bender lets creators describe a sound and pull it out of a finished mix, then explore variations on an interactive canvas. Creators can shape a sound in real time, match its movement to a video, or start from a description and create something new.

Images and design

Project Deep Brush

This is one you can experiment with now. Project Deep Brush uses AI to understand an image’s shape, color, and lighting. Brushstrokes can follow the contours of a surface, colors can be changed while preserving natural shadows, and light can be painted directly into a scene.

Project Sight Span

Ever wish you'd framed something differently? Project Sight Span transforms an image into a navigable environment that creators can step inside and explore, finding new angles and composing shots beyond the original frame.

Project Hands On

Project Hands On uses AI to understand what’s in an image and creates controls directly on the canvas so creators can manipulate elements of a scene by hand.

Project Rinse Repeat

Project Rinse Repeat captures the edits made in one part of an image and applies them to another, adapting them to the new area. Because the edits are recreated with native Photoshop tools, they remain editable.

Project Link Up

Project Link Up explores how a creator’s gestures can express intent and bring design elements together. Drag a car into an illustrated parking space, for example, and the project adapts its perspective, scale, and style to fit the scene. The result is editable vector artwork.

Sneaks hit rate

Adobe says that approximately half of the projects shown in any given year go on to feature in final software. Which of this year’s projects will is, of course, as yet unknown. But one of the goals of Sneaks is to gauge reaction to new tools and techniques. Judging by the audience reaction to Project Deep Brush and Project Hands On, not to mention their debut in Adobe Labs Playground, chances of them appearing in full down the line would seem to be pretty high.

entry.title: Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone: specs and price
entry.summary: 1 minute read Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone: specs and price 2:44 Blackmagic Design’s new Ambisonic Microphone packs 108 MEMS microphones into a palm-sized 7th order array that records spatial audio over one USB-C cable. Blackmagic Design is doubling down on the immersive video
entry.content:
1 minute read
Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone: specs and price
2:44

Blackmagic Design’s new Ambisonic Microphone packs 108 MEMS microphones into a palm-sized 7th order array that records spatial audio over one USB-C cable.

Blackmagic Design is doubling down on the immersive video product line started with the release of the URSA Cine Immersive by adding audio to the mix. The Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone is a 7th order ambisonic microphone array with 108 digital MEMS microphones that are positioned in a sphere to capture the entire sound field in all directions.

The microphones are mounted flush in a solid, faceted metal body small enough to fit in the palm of your hand and mount on a camera.

7th order ambisonics

And in case you were wondering, ‘7th order’ describes how precisely a mic can pin down where a sound comes from. The rule of thumb is that a mic needs at least (order + 1) squared capsules: four for 1st order, nine for 2nd, and so on. At 7th order that works out to 64 channels, which is what the Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone outputs.

As far as we can tell, this is the highest-order commercial mic available, with the only higher-order mics confined to R&D.

“This microphone started when we were collaborating with Apple on the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive camera. I heard a high resolution spatial audio capture for the first time and it was like hearing an acoustic reality, I was totally blown away,” says Grant Petty, Blackmagic Design CEO. “Apple licensed their array geometry and the ambisonic encoding filters, we did the engineering and design, and the result is an ambisonic microphone where you just plug in one cable and capture true spatial audio.”

One cable, built-in encoding, no breakout box

An internal processor running Apple’s encoding filters converts all 108 microphones to 7th order ambisonics in real time, so no encoding software or breakout box is needed.

Impressively, given all that complexity, the mic connects and is powered over a single USB-C cable. That helps it mount on the Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive and record spatial audio directly into the camera’s immersive files for Apple Immersive content. It also works with a computer for recording and live mixing in Fairlight Live, and even records directly to iPhone using the Blackmagic Camera app. A USB to SMPTE-2110 converter will be available for broadcast workflows.

Pricing and availability

The microphone will be available in December 2026 for $1695 excluding local duties and taxes. Blackmagic lists it at $1909 in the US, which includes duties. The $2405 Blackmagic Ambisonic Microphone Kit adds a dedicated Microphone Mount, a windshield, and a locking USB-C cable for secure attachment.

Adobe Firefly Build a story and video assembler
3:18

Two new beta workspaces in Firefly take an idea to planned scenes and shots, then on to an assembled short video.

Adobe has added two beta workspaces to Firefly at MAX 2026 that between them cover the journey from idea to short video. Build a story, found under Video in the Firefly menu, turns a prompt into a structured visual story. Assemble short video then offers a simplified, single-track workspace for arranging the clips.

Build a story: from idea to shot cards

For anyone who pootled around with prompts in the early days of AI, the rate of change is jaw-dropping. Users can now describe an idea to the Firefly AI Assistant, which asks for a target duration and optional details on characters, locations, objects, and creative direction.

It then proposes a look, a sound approach, the number of scenes and shots, and the characters, locations, and objects involved. Once the proposal is accepted, the assistant saves those characters, locations, and objects as elements to keep them consistent across shots, wires them into the relevant shots, writes a beat description for each, and generates a first frame.

Shots appear as cards grouped by scene, each showing its first frame. Frames and beat descriptions can be refined in the Shot editor or by asking the assistant, and clips can be generated card by card or for every card at once with Generate all. The finished sequence can be downloaded or opened in Timeline (beta) for further editing. One catch: resolution and aspect ratio can’t be changed for any shot once frames are generated.

The Creative Agent behind the assistant also gains Plan Mode, a Model Selector, and saved preferences for formats, colors, brand guidelines, characters, and products.

Assemble short video: a single-track workspace

Assemble short video is a lightweight workspace for generated or imported clips on a single track. Users can trim, split, and rearrange clips, adjust the volume of individual clips, detect cuts, and change the aspect ratio. Selected clips can be regenerated from a text prompt, with an optional reference image, and a cost indicator shows the generative credits required before generation starts. Regenerated versions appear as takes to compare, and the sequence can be sent to Timeline (beta) for multi-track editing.

It can be reached from Video > Assemble short video, after a Quick Action workflow, or from the AI Assistant after generating with an omni model.

A year of Firefly video work

These new tools extend a year of Firefly video work. The browser-based video editor was announced in private beta at MAX 2025 and opened in public beta that December, Quick Cut added automatic first-draft assembly in February, and Adobe announced storyboard-to-video generation in June.

Availability and limits

Both tools are in beta, and Adobe’s help pages say neither is available to Creative Cloud for Teams or Enterprise users. Build a story works only in Chrome and Edge on desktop, doesn’t support viewports smaller than 1080 x 700 pixels, and takes clips only from Adobe cloud storage’s generation history, not direct uploads. That leaves Build a story limited in scope for now.

Adobe Disney AI alliance and Google partnership
2:34

Adobe is now Disney’s Official AI Innovation Partner, with custom Firefly Foundry models at the core. It has also deepened its Google partnership.

Adobe has announced two partnerships at MAX 2026 with Disney and Google that between them cover both ends of its AI strategy: bespoke models for a major studio, and a wider choice of off-the-shelf models for everyone else.

Disney: custom models and early access

On Monday, Adobe and The Walt Disney Company announced a multi-year strategic alliance that makes Adobe an Official AI Innovation Partner of Disney. Adobe will give Disney early access to Firefly, Firefly Foundry, Premiere, and Photoshop, along with dedicated engineering and research resources to support the Disney production pipeline.

The centerpiece of the deal is Firefly Foundry, Adobe’s service for proprietary models. Disney will work with Adobe on generative models tailored to its properties, trained on character attributes, environments, and visual styles. Walt Disney Imagineering Research & Development is already using it in the theme park pipeline, with a sketch-to-image model that turns hand-drawn concepts into rendered 2D concept art, and a custom image model that generates franchise-accurate assets.

There’s further integration across other parts of the sprawling Disney empire too, but perhaps what makes this most interesting is Disney’s track record with AI. The House of Mouse inked a high-profile deal with OpenAI that tanked when OpenAI pulled the plug on its Sora video app. It will have searched very carefully before putting its eggs into the AI basket once more, and getting Disney on board is a definite feather in Adobe’s cap.

Google: models in, tools out

Then, on Tuesday, Adobe and Google announced an expanded partnership running in both directions. Google’s latest image and video models will continue to reach Firefly, Photoshop, Express, and Premiere, with Gemini Omni, Veo, and Nano Banana already available to customers. Gemini models will also help power AI features in Acrobat.

In the other direction, Acrobat will come to Google Workspace through Drive and Gmail, Adobe’s connectors in Gemini and Gemini Enterprise will expand to include Acrobat and more creative tools, and Adobe’s creative tools will arrive in Google Search’s AI Mode. Adobe and Google DeepMind will also explore a customized Google image model for Photoshop that could allow near-real-time prompt edits with a choice of variants.
